newsitem.title: UK: Police condemn N.Irish guerrilla mine.
newsitem.headline: Police condemn N.Irish guerrilla mine.

text.p: Police said a suspected IRA anti-personnel mine found near Dungannon town in Northern Ireland on Friday was "very lethal" and would have killed or maimed if it had exploded.

In Belfast, U.S. politician William Weld, governor of Massachusetts, who was leading a trade delegation, gave a warning that violence and the collapse of peace efforts in the British province was a disincentive to foreign investment.
After talks with parties including Sinn Fein, the political wing of the Irish Republican Army, Weld told reporters he sensed that "everyone understands that violence is anathema to investment".
Weld said he wanted to encourge trade with the province. He would like to see a fresh IRA ceasefire and participation by its Sinn Fein political wing in peace talks.

The province had many positive investment aspects but their potential was clouded by last year's failure of an IRA truce "and the side-tracking of the peace process" which he said made investors, tourists and business people very nervous.

Security sources said they suspected that the mine, which contained high explosive, scrap metal and petrol, was the work of guerrillas targetting police officers who had been searching the area this week for the body of a murdered woman.

No organisation claimed responsibility for the device which was disarmed by British bomb disposal officers. Security sources said it had the hallmarks of the IRA which is fighting to end British rule.
Police Superintendent Basil Kerr said the device, left at head height in a tree, was in a well frequented area.
"Anyone that was in its path would have certainly died or suffered very serious injuries," he told BBC radio.
In an unconnected operation, police officers had searched an area nearby on Monday night and found a woman's body the following day, she said.

"We are extremely angry and annoyed that (while) carrying out our normal investigations someone slips into the background and places a cowardly device to catch us...or indeed innocent civilians who happen to be in the area at the time," Kerr said.
IRA guerrillas have used a wide variety of home-made mortars and other bombs in an escalating war against British forces.
Britain says the guerrillas must abandon hostilities before Sinn Fein can be be given a seat in talks.
